name: Cenegermin
lead: Cenegermin (brand name Oxervate) is a recombinant human nerve growth factor (rhNGF) given as an eye drop, produced in E. coli. It acts on the TrkA and p75NTR receptors and was the first drug approved for neurotrophic keratitis, a rare condition in which damaged corneal nerves lead to persistent epithelial defects [4][8]. The European Union approved it in 2017 and the United States in 2018 [7].

In the registration trials, most adults with moderate or severe neurotrophic keratitis reached complete corneal healing within eight weeks, with healing rates generally higher than with vehicle [4]. The most common adverse effects are eye pain, inflammation, increased tearing, eyelid pain and a foreign-body sensation [7].

Cenegermin is a medical eye treatment. No published work describes it as an appearance product. It sits in the recovery category because it supports healing of damaged corneal tissue, and anyone looking at eye health and eye appearance will find it as the corneal-surface healing drug that restores a clear, intact cornea when nerve damage has broken down the surface.[1][4]

paras: Nerve growth factor (NGF) was discovered in the 1950s by Rita Levi-Montalcini and Stanley Cohen at Washington University in St. Louis, building on preliminary work by Levi-Montalcini and Hertha Meyer in Rio de Janeiro in 1952. Their 1954 publication established the protein, and the pair shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.[17] NGF regulates the growth, maintenance and survival of sensory and sympathetic neurons, acting through the TrkA receptor, which activates the Ras/MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways, and through p75NTR, which depending on context can promote survival or cell death.[17]

The cornea is among the most densely innervated tissues in the body, and corneal nerves have both sensory and trophic roles. Reviews describe neurotrophic keratopathy as a condition in which reduced or absent corneal sensation impairs the trophic function of the nerves, leaving the epithelium prone to breakdown and, in severe cases, stromal melting and perforation.[1] Many systemic and ocular conditions, including surgery, preserved medications and herpes simplex virus infection, can lead to it.[1][20] A paediatric review lists congenital and acquired causes and notes that, before cenegermin, treatments in children included lubrication, serum drops and surgical corneal neurotization, which routes a donor nerve to the anaesthetic cornea.[19]

The approved indication is neurotrophic keratitis (also called neurotrophic keratopathy), in which reduced or absent corneal sensation impairs the trophic function of sensory nerves and leaves the epithelium prone to breakdown and the stroma to melting [1]. Existing treatments have mainly been supportive, and cenegermin was introduced to address the underlying nerve-related problem [3].

Cenegermin is a recombinant human beta-NGF (residues 1-118) produced in E. coli and formulated as an eye drop; Wikipedia describes it as a peripherally selective agonist of TrkA and p75NTR.[7] Wikipedia's NGF article describes it as a 0.002 percent eye drop and notes that mouse NGF has been a licensed medicine in China since 2003.[17] The drug is prescribed and supervised by eye doctors; this article does not cover dosing.

A multicenter, randomized, double-masked, vehicle-controlled trial (NGF0214) in 11 US sites randomized 48 patients with a neurotrophic persistent epithelial defect to cenegermin 20 micrograms per millilitre or vehicle, with six drops daily for eight weeks [2]. A Drugs review of the registration trials reported that most adults achieved complete healing after up to eight weeks, with higher rates than vehicle [4]. Follow-up reports have examined corneal nerves and sensitivity over eight months and longer-term clinical efficacy [9][10]. A NICE single technology appraisal evidence review assessed it from a cost-effectiveness perspective [11].

In the NGF0214 pivotal trial, patients were followed for 24 weeks after the eight-week masked treatment, and the primary endpoint was healing of the neurotrophic lesion at eight weeks, judged by masked central readers using fluorescein staining.[2] An eight-month follow-up of corneal nerves and sensitivity, and a 2023 study of corneal nerve regeneration, examined whether the drug is associated with changes in subbasal nerve morphology and sensitivity.[9][21] A 2019 Clinical Ophthalmology update noted that prior medical and surgical treatments were supportive and poorly addressed the underlying corneal anaesthesia, which is the gap cenegermin was developed for.[3]
Common adverse effects reported are eye pain, ocular inflammation, increased tearing, eyelid pain and a feeling of a foreign body in the eye [7].

Beyond the pivotal randomized trial and its follow-ups above [2][9][10], ClinicalTrials.gov lists further registered studies: a recruiting phase 3 trial of intranasal cenegermin in non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NCT07453888) [12], a phase 3 trial in persistent corneal epithelial defect (NCT07519902) [13], a completed phase 3 trial in severe Sjogren's dry eye disease (NCT05136170) [14], a completed phase 2 trial of rhNGF in moderate to severe dry eye (NCT03982368) [15], and a completed phase 4 study in stage 1 neurotrophic keratitis (NCT04485546) [16]. No studies of cenegermin for cosmetic or appearance purposes were found.

A phase 2, randomised, vehicle-controlled, dose-ranging trial in moderate-to-severe dry eye disease was published in BMC Ophthalmology in 2024; its authors note that dry eye includes neurosensory abnormalities and that NGF is important for maintaining corneal nerve integrity.[18] A 2025 review of approved and upcoming dry eye treatments lists the established approved options for that condition, and cenegermin is not among them.[22]
Cenegermin is prescription-only in the US, EU, Canada and Australia [7].

Wikipedia describes cenegermin as the first-in-class drug of its kind approved by the FDA, and lists it among orphan drugs, reflecting the rarity of neurotrophic keratitis.[7] A UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence appraisal reviewed it, with a University of Liverpool evidence review group assessing the manufacturer's submission on clinical and cost-effectiveness; the manufacturer is Dompe.[11]

card.summary: A prescription nerve growth factor eye drop approved for a rare corneal disease, with no appearance use.
card.note: Approved only for neurotrophic keratitis; no cosmetic studies.

quick.overview:
Cenegermin (Oxervate) is a recombinant human nerve growth factor eye drop approved in the EU in 2017 and the US in 2018 for neurotrophic keratitis, a rare corneal nerve disease.

Trials in that condition showed most patients healing within about eight weeks. It is not an appearance product, and no cosmetic studies were found.
quick.mechanism: It acts on the TrkA and p75NTR receptors and was developed to address the nerve-related cause of corneal breakdown rather than only support the surface.
quick.risks: Reported adverse effects include eye pain, inflammation, tearing, eyelid pain and foreign-body sensation. It is prescription-only.

chain: rhNGF eye drops act on TrkA and p75NTR receptors in the cornea
Corneal epithelium heals in neurotrophic keratitis
Clear, intact corneal surface and preserved vision
angle.text: Cenegermin is a prescribed healing drug for a rare corneal disease. Its link to appearance is through eye health: a healed cornea preserves a clear, comfortable eye, but it is not used to change how healthy eyes look.
